claims.text: That is the **shape of a live object**, and for this repo it dissolves a named blindness: ``structcore``'s own index travels as a bare ``dict``, so the most important data structure in the tree is invisible to any declaration-level pass.
claims.why: No code in this chunk references 'structcore' or its index; cannot verify.

claims.text: Nothing here reads an element, a cell, a row or a scalar payload. It records metadata — concrete class, dtype, shape, strides, contiguity, byte size, and KEY or COLUMN NAMES.
claims.why: This chunk only defines constants and helpers; no actual observation logic is present to verify the claim.

claims.text: Because getting a live object means the program RAN. ``structcore`` is a static pass by construction and ``tools/vet.py`` states the rule outright: you do not run untrusted code to decide anything about it.
claims.why: No code in this chunk references 'structcore' or 'tools/vet.py'; cannot verify.

claims.text: So observation is a separate, opt-in lane that *feeds* the graph with edges stamped ``provenance=observed`` — it is never part of an index build, and it runs only on trees the operator owns.
claims.why: No code in this chunk implements observation or provenance; cannot verify.

claims.text: ``(1000, 3)`` is the shape this input produced. It is not the shape the function requires. A field never seen is not a field that cannot appear. Every record carries ``provenance="observed"`` and the run it came from, and any consumer that reports it as a fact is wrong — the same discipline ``eval/ceiling.py`` applies when it separates its clean arm from its leaky one.
claims.why: No code in this chunk defines provenance or references 'eval/ceiling.py'; cannot verify.

claims.text: Duck-typed throughout: numpy, pandas, h5py and uproot are probed by attribute, never imported. A tree without them degrades to the generic families and says so.
claims.why: No code in this chunk performs any probing or imports; cannot verify duck-typing claim.

claims.text: A dict with 40 000 keys is described by its first ``MAX_NAMES`` and a count, never by all of them: an unbounded descriptor is how an observer becomes the memory problem it was meant to diagnose.
claims.why: Constant MAX_NAMES is defined as 64, but no observation code is present to verify that only first 64 keys are used.

claims.text: ``getattr(obj, "columns", ()) or ()`` looks harmless and raises on a pandas Index, whose ``__bool__`` refuses to answer. Any observer that touches array-likes has to fetch attributes without asking whether they are truthy.
claims.why: The _attr function uses getattr with a default and returns default if None, avoiding truthiness check on the attribute value itself. This matches the described behavior.

observations.what: Shape dataclass is defined with only three fields: family, type_name, dtype. The docstring claims it records shape, strides, contiguity, byte size, and key/column names, but those fields are not present in this chunk.

Helper function _human_bytes has a bug: in the loop, when unit == 'TiB', it returns n as if it were already divided, but the loop divides n by 1024 each iteration. For 1024^4 bytes, n after three divisions is 1024, so it returns '1024.0 GiB' instead of '1.0 TiB'. The condition should check if n < 1024 before dividing.
No imports for numpy, pandas, h5py, or uproot are present in this chunk, consistent with the duck-typing claim, but no probing code exists yet.
